images.title: Biggest jumps come early
images.purpose: Show how growth between successive ages is found as the step from one height to the next, and that the steps are largest in the first years.
images.composition: A rising staircase of six columns centred in the frame, with the first and last steps highlighted; generous white space above.
exact_structure: Exactly 6 vertical teal (#0072B2) columns standing on one grey (#6B7280) baseline, labelled under the baseline birth, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, with the caption age in years below them.
Only the first and last columns carry their values on top: 50 and 107.
The top part of the age 1 column, from height 50 up to its top at 75, is filled reddish purple (#CC79A7) and labelled +25 beside it.
The top part of the age 5 column, from height 101 up to its top at 107, is filled amber (#E69F00) and labelled +6 beside it.
All other columns are plain teal with no value or step label.
Arithmetic check for the reviewer only, NOT drawn in the frame: 75 − 50 = 25 and 107 − 101 = 6.
rejection: columns not rising from left to right
images.takeaway: Growth per year is the difference between successive heights, and young children grow fastest.
images.description: Six rising columns from 50 cm at birth to 107 cm at age 5, the first step of 25 highlighted in purple and the last step of 6 in amber.
images.context: Shown beside the concept text and video for this concept.
images.teaching_notes: Ask students why the first step is so much taller than the last before they compare the 2019 columns.

image_decisions.why: A staircase makes year to year growth visible as differences.
